learning.javascript:
Strings can't be changed: build a new one

JavaScript strings are immutable: once made, a string never changes. Assigning to s[0] doesn't change s (it's ignored, or in strict mode it throws a TypeError). Instead, build a new string from pieces. + puts two strings together into a new one (concatenation), and leaves both pieces as they were:

const word = "h" + "I";      // "hI": a new string
const louder = word + "!";   // "hI!": another new string
                             // word is still "hI"
learning.python:
Strings can't be changed: build a new one

Python strings are immutable: once made, a string never changes. s[0] = "H" raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. Instead, build a new string from pieces. + puts two strings together into a new one (concatenation), and leaves both pieces as they were:

word = "h" + "I"            # "hI": a new string
louder = word + "!"         # "hI!": another new string
                            # word is still "hI"
learning.cpp:
A std::string can be changed

Unlike strings in JavaScript, Python, Java and D, a C++ std::string is mutable: s[0] = 'H'; changes it. Here s is passed by value, so the function has its own copy, and you can change it and return it. But changing it in place only replaces characters, and an answer longer than s needs a new string. + puts two strings together into a new one (concatenation), and leaves both pieces as they were:

string h = "h";
string word = h + "I";        // "hI": a new string
string louder = word + "!";   // "hI!": another new string
                              // word is still "hI"

Careful with two string literals: "h" + "I" doesn't compile (“invalid operands … to binary 'operator+'”). A literal in quotes is an array of chars, not a std::string, and at least one side of + must be a std::string. That's why the example starts with string h.

See operator+ on cppreference.
learning.java:
Strings can't be changed: build a new one

Java Strings are immutable: once made, a String never changes, and there's no method that changes one. Build a new one instead. + puts two Strings together into a new one (concatenation), and leaves both pieces as they were:

String word = "h" + "I";        // "hI": a new String
String louder = word + "!";     // "hI!": another new String
                                // word is still "hI"

See String in the Java 21 documentation.
learning.d:
Strings can't be changed: build a new one

In D, string means immutable(char)[]: an array of characters that can't be changed, so s[0] = 'H'; doesn't compile. Build a new one instead. ~ puts two strings together into a new one (concatenation), and leaves both pieces as they were:

string word = "h" ~ "I";      // "hI": a new string
string louder = word ~ "!";   // "hI!": another new string
                              // word is still "hI"

See Strings and concatenation in the D language specification.
